questions.q: What is the main structural difference between one large agent holding every tool and a multi-agent system?
options: A multi-agent system splits the work across several agents, each with a narrower role, its own tool set, and its own context
Multi-agent systems are not allowed to use any tools at all
There is no real difference — the terms describe the same architecture
A multi-agent system requires exactly two agents, never more or fewer
questions.explain: Rather than one generalist juggling every tool and role in a single shared context, a multi-agent system gives each agent a focused scope of its own.

questions.q: In the Claude Agent SDK, what do subagents actually provide that makes multi-agent coordination practical?
options: They all share one single, combined context with the main agent, with no separation
Subagents are purely a marketing term with no functional mechanism behind them
Separate context from the main agent, so only a subagent's distilled outcome comes back rather than every intermediate step
Subagents can only be defined through a paid add-on service
questions.explain: A subagent doing deep research doesn't flood the main agent's context with every search result — separate context is the actual mechanism, not just an implementation detail.

questions.q: In the three-agent research/write/review example, why does the writer agent not see the research agent's raw search results directly?
options: Because the writer agent is forbidden from ever producing any text
Because research and writer are actually the exact same agent under a different name
Because raw search results are always classified and cannot be shared with any agent
Because each agent's context stays scoped to its own job — the writer receives the research agent's distilled findings, not its raw intermediate output
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 11's high-signal principle for tool output, now applied to what one agent hands off to another — only what's needed, not everything generated along the way.

questions.q: What real cost does this lesson say multi-agent systems introduce that a single agent doesn't have?
options: Multi-agent systems have zero additional costs compared to a single agent
Coordination: managing who talks to whom, in what order, and how disagreements between agents get resolved
Multi-agent systems eliminate the need for any tool schemas whatsoever
Multi-agent systems are always strictly cheaper in tokens than a single agent
questions.explain: Splitting work doesn't remove complexity — it moves it into coordinating separate agents that each only see part of the picture, which is a cost worth paying only when roles are genuinely separable.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does a multi-agent system actually earn its added complexity?
options: Whenever a task simply feels big or important
Never — multi-agent systems are always a worse choice than one large agent
Only when the task involves exactly three agents, no more and no fewer
When roles are genuinely separable with clean hand-offs between them
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that bigness alone doesn't justify the coordination overhead — separable roles with clean hand-offs are what make the tradeoff worthwhile.
